items.title: The first theorem proved by computer
items.claim: Conjectured in 1852: any map can be coloured with 4 colours so no neighbouring regions share a colour. Proved by Appel and Haken in 1976 — using 1200 hours of computer time and case-by-case verification. Mathematicians argued for years about whether it counted.
items.prompt: Why was the computer proof controversial?

options.text: Computers were not allowed to do mathematics
The proof reduced the problem to 1936 'unavoidable configurations' and checked each by computer; no human could read the entire proof, and verification depended on trusting the computer code
The proof contained a subtle error

items.reveal:
The four-colour theorem was first conjectured by Francis Guthrie in 1852. Numerous false proofs were published (including Kempe's 1879 'proof', which stood for 11 years before Heawood found the gap).

Appel and Haken (University of Illinois) reduced the problem to checking that 1936 configurations were 'reducible'. A computer ran the checks over 1200 hours.

Mathematicians' objections: a proof is supposed to be readable, checkable and persuasive to humans. This one wasn't.

Follow-up proofs simplified the configurations (Robertson, Sanders, Seymour, Thomas, 1996: 633 cases) and have been formally verified by proof assistants (Gonthier, 2005, using Coq). Most mathematicians now accept the theorem, though some retain reservations about computer-assisted proofs in general.

It set the template for many later computer-assisted proofs: the Kepler conjecture (Hales, 2014), the Boolean Pythagorean triples problem (200 terabytes of evidence).
items.why: Proof is imagined as a human activity. Computer-assisted proof is a hybrid form that still divides mathematical philosophy — what is a proof, who certifies it, who is it for?

items.title: The sum of all positive integers equals minus one twelfth
items.claim: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + ... = -1/12. This obviously fails as a normal sum (it diverges to infinity). But it is the value of the Riemann zeta function analytically continued to s = -1, and it shows up in physics (Casimir effect, string theory).
items.prompt: How does an obviously divergent sum get a finite value?

options.text: Analytic continuation extends a function defined on one domain (where the series converges) to a larger domain (where the series doesn't); zeta(-1) is well-defined as a function value even though the corresponding series diverges
Negative numbers were added without permission

items.reveal_title: Ramanujan, Hardy, and the strange identity
items.reveal:
Srinivasa Ramanujan wrote to Hardy in 1913 claiming results like 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + ... = -1/12. Hardy initially thought Ramanujan must be a crank — until he checked.

The Riemann zeta function is defined by zeta(s) = sum from n=1 to infinity of 1/n to the power s, but only when the real part of s exceeds 1. The function extends analytically to the whole complex plane (except a pole at s = 1). At s = -1, zeta(-1) = -1/12.

If you formally substitute s = -1 into the series, you get 1 + 2 + 3 + ... The series doesn't converge there — but the function it defined still has a value, just by a different (analytic continuation) method.

In quantum field theory, the same -1/12 appears. The Casimir force calculation involves summing zero-point energies of standing waves; this sum diverges, but the physical answer obtained by zeta regularisation matches experiment.

The identity is not casually 'true' as arithmetic. It's true as the value of a specific extension of the zeta function — and that extension happens to give physically correct predictions.
items.why: Treating divergent sums as if they have finite values seems like a trick — but in the right framework, analytic continuation gives them precise meanings that physics turns out to use.

items.title: The most important open problem in mathematics
items.claim: Riemann conjectured in 1859 that all non-trivial zeros of the zeta function lie on the line Re(s) = 1/2. The conjecture controls the distribution of primes among integers. Proving (or disproving) it has been unsolved for 165 years.
items.prompt: Why do we care about complex zeros of a strange function?

options.text: The distribution of prime numbers is encoded in the zeros of the Riemann zeta function — proving the Riemann hypothesis would establish a vast number of theorems in number theory that are currently conditional on it
It tells us the value of zeta at integer points
It's part of the definition of pi

items.reveal:
Riemann's only paper on number theory (1859) defined the analytic continuation of the zeta function and noted that the function has 'trivial zeros' at -2, -4, -6, ... and other 'non-trivial zeros' in the strip 0 less than Re(s) less than 1. He conjectured all non-trivial zeros lie exactly on Re(s) = 1/2.

The Prime Number Theorem (Hadamard, de la Vallée Poussin, 1896) says the count of primes up to x is asymptotically x / ln x. The Riemann hypothesis would tighten the error term enormously.

Thousands of theorems in modern number theory are stated 'assuming RH'. A proof would make them unconditional. Conversely, a disproof would force major rewrites.

The first 10 trillion non-trivial zeros have all been computed and verified to lie on Re(s) = 1/2 (Gourdon, 2004). This doesn't prove the hypothesis.

The Clay Mathematics Institute lists it as one of seven Millennium Prize Problems, with a $1,000,000 reward. So far, only Poincaré (Perelman, 2003) has been solved.
items.why: Primes look like a chaotic distribution. The Riemann hypothesis says they have hidden, beautiful regularity controlled by complex analysis — and 165 years of effort haven't proved or disproved it.
